headline: Agriculture was humanity's biggest revolution—it created civilization itself
universal_truth: Surplus creates specialization; when basic needs are met, new possibilities emerge
fun_facts: Agriculture began independently in at least 7 different places around 10,000 years ago
Before farming, humans spent most of their time finding food—farming freed time for other pursuits
Early farmers were actually less healthy than hunter-gatherers—but farming enabled population growth
discussion_questions: What became possible because not everyone had to find food?
What did humans lose when they stopped hunting and gathering?
How might civilization be different without agriculture?

hook.script: For 200,000 years, humans hunted and gathered—following food wherever it led. Then, about 10,000 years ago, we started growing food instead of finding it. This single change created everything: cities, writing, technology, civilization itself.

cliff.script: Growing food sounds simpler than hunting it. So why is agriculture considered the most important revolution in human history? What changed because of farming?

options.text: Food surplus meant not everyone had to farm—freeing people to specialize in other skills
options.response: Yes. Surplus is the key. When farmers produce more than they eat, others can become builders, artists, priests, and scholars. Specialization creates civilization.

options.text: Farming provided a more reliable food source than hunting
options.response: Reliability helped, but the deeper change was surplus enabling specialization...

fact1.title: Surplus Society
fact1.script: Hunter-gatherers spend most time finding food—no surplus, no specialists. Farming changed this. One farmer can feed many. Surplus food allowed some people to do other things: build, govern, create, think. Civilization grew from agricultural surplus.

fact2.title: Settlement Begins
fact2.script: Farming requires staying in one place—tending crops through seasons. Permanent settlements became villages, then cities. Writing emerged to track harvests and trade. Agriculture anchored humans to land and created the concept of home.

fact3.title: Trade-offs
fact3.script: Early farmers were actually shorter and less healthy than hunter-gatherers—diets narrowed, diseases spread in dense settlements. But farming supported larger populations. Health declined; numbers grew. The trade-off shaped everything after.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Surplus creates specialization. When basic needs are met, new possibilities emerge. Agriculture freed humans from constant food-seeking—and that freedom built everything we call civilization.

outro.script: That's Day 134. Tomorrow, we'll explore how animals are related. Until then, appreciate that civilization exists because farmers could grow more food than they needed.

growTrack.title: Specialization Reflection - What Would You Do?
growTrack.activity: You have a specialized skill because you don't have to find food all day. What would you do differently if you spent 8 hours daily hunting and gathering? Agricultural surplus gave you choices. What are you doing with them?
